note: Cold War-shaped relations.
Non-aligned: on cordial terms with both blocs and neither's client.
Bonn's warmth here is what makes its later push for recognition bite.

Brazil: friendly with everyone and committed to nobody. The 1980s debt crisis is what Washington means to Brasilia, so the warmth is real but thin, and the Latin American nuclear rivalry with Argentina ended at Guadalajara in 1991.

Indonesia: an anti-communist client of the West since 1965, and Japan's largest aid recipient. Relations with Beijing were suspended outright in 1967 over the coup and are only restored in August 1990 — which is why they start negative and have to be repaired.

Egypt post-Camp David: the peace with Israel is cold but eleven years old, and it bought Cairo a permanent American subsidy. The suspension from the Arab League ended in 1989 and Egypt sits with Iraq in the Arab Cooperation Council as the game opens — Cairo's turn against Baghdad in August is a choice the sim has to make, not a fact it starts with.

Israel: the American relationship is the deepest in the game. Moscow broke relations in 1967 and does not restore them until October 1991, even as it lets its Jews leave. Ankara is the one Muslim capital with full ties.

Turkey in NATO: forty years in the alliance, two million of its people working in Germany, and Incirlik. Baghdad is a customer, not a friend — the Kirkuk-Yumurtalik pipeline is Iraq's main outlet and Ozal shuts it in August 1990.
Nigeria: Commonwealth ties to London, oil ties to Washington, and the non-aligned habits of a country that has led African diplomacy since independence.

Vietnam post-Cambodia: the last troops came home in September 1989 but nothing has been forgiven. Washington's embargo is fifteen years old and has four more to run; Beijing fought a border war in 1979, kept shelling into 1988, and sank three Vietnamese ships off Johnson Reef that March. Moscow is the patron whose money stops arriving this year.

Spain, four years into the European Community and eight into NATO. Warm with the Community it joined on 1 January 1986 and whose structural funds were rebuilding it, and warm-but-reserved with Washington: the 1988 base agreement was a renegotiation that expelled the 401st Tactical Fighter Wing from Torrejon, which is why the number here sits below Italy's 60 rather than beside it.

London is the outlier and Gibraltar is the reason. The Brussels Declaration of 1984 reopened the frontier and opened a negotiating process that went nowhere; the two are NATO allies who do not agree about a border. A positive but thin line, which is the shape of a grievance that is real and is never going to be a war.
Latin America is the other axis of Spanish foreign policy in this period — the first Ibero-American Summit met at Guadalajara in July 1991 on a Spanish initiative.

The Netherlands: the most reliably Atlanticist government in continental Europe and one of the least Atlanticist electorates. The cruise-missile decision of 1979 produced the largest demonstrations in Dutch history - 400,000 people in The Hague in October 1983 - and the word Hollanditis was coined in Washington for it; the missiles were accepted anyway in November 1985. The Washington number reflects the government, which is what this model has.

Benelux is the warmest dyad in this file at 70. The Belgium-Netherlands-Luxembourg customs union of 1948 predates the Coal and Steel Community, and the two states had already abolished their mutual frontier before anyone drafted Schengen.

Jakarta is the outlier and decolonisation is the reason. The Netherlands fought two wars to keep Indonesia between 1945 and 1949, gave up western New Guinea only in 1962, and by 1990 was tying its aid to human rights in East Timor. Suharto dissolved the Dutch-chaired aid consortium and refused all Dutch assistance in March 1992; a thin positive line here is the year before that.

Belgium hosts NATO headquarters at Evere and the European Commission at Brussels, which makes it structurally incapable of being anybody's opponent. Paris slightly ahead of Bonn and London because half the country speaks French and the Francophone parties were in government.

Sweden is non-aligned in peace and neutral in war, and the numbers have to show that it is not simply a quieter NATO member. Washington at 35 rather than the 55-65 the alliance members carry: Olof Palme marched in Stockholm behind the North Vietnamese ambassador in 1968, Sweden recognised the Provisional Revolutionary Government in 1969, and the United States withdrew its ambassador and left the post vacant from 1972 to 1974. Relations were correct by 1990 and had never been warm since.

Moscow at 10, positive and very thin. Sweden traded with the Soviet Union and voted against it at the United Nations, and spent the 1980s hunting submarines in its own archipelago - the Whiskey-class boat that grounded inside the Karlskrona naval base on 27 October 1981 is the incident everyone remembers, and it was not the only one.

The Nordic three at 70 are the highest cluster in the file after Benelux. The Nordic Council dates from 1952, the passport union and the common labour market from 1954; the four of them disagreed about NATO and agreed about everything else.

Hanoi at 40 is not sentiment. Sweden was the first Western country to establish full diplomatic relations with North Vietnam, in January 1969, and paid for the Bai Bang paper mill in Vinh Phu through the whole war and after it - the largest single aid project Sweden ever funded.

Switzerland is the one state in this region that is not in the European Community, not in NATO, and - until 10 September 2002 - not in the United Nations either, having voted 75.7% against joining in the referendum of 16 March 1986. Every number here is therefore a trade and banking relationship rather than an alliance, which is why nothing reaches the 55-65 the Community members show each other.

Vienna at 60 is the exception and is the closest thing Switzerland has to a peer: the other permanently neutral Alpine German-speaking republic, and the only capital in Europe whose foreign-policy position Bern never had to explain.

Austria's neutrality was the price of the State Treaty of 15 May 1955 and the Soviet withdrawal, and it was written into constitutional law in October of that year on Moscow's insistence. That is why the Moscow number here, 25, is the highest any non-communist state in this file shows the Soviet Union except Finland's: Vienna was where the two blocs met, from the Kennedy-Khrushchev summit of 1961 to the SALT II signature of 1979, and it was a neutrality Moscow had bought and therefore valued.

Bonn at 65 is the highest single number in this block and needs no elaborate defence - same language, an economy fused with the German one, a currency pegged to the D-mark since 1976, and an Anschluss that both states spent the post-war period declining to discuss.

Rome at 45 and not higher: South Tyrol. The dispute went to the United Nations General Assembly in 1960 and 1961, produced a bombing campaign, and was formally declared settled by Austria only on 11 June 1992. Two European neighbours with a live minority question at the United Nations do not sit at 55.

Belgrade at 45 because Austria had been the loudest Western advocate of Slovene and Croat interests since before the federation began to fail, and because Yugoslav guest workers and their families had made Vienna a Yugoslav city as much as a German one.

Portugal and the United Kingdom at 60 is the oldest live alliance in the world. The Treaty of Windsor was signed on 9 May 1386 and has never been abrogated; Salazar granted the Azores to the Royal Air Force under it in 1943 while remaining neutral, and Lisbon was still granting Lajes to the Americans on the same logic in 1990. Washington at 55 is that base and little else - the agreement was renewed in 1983 for a term running to 1991.

Brasilia at 65 is the highest number in this block. Portuguese is the language of 150m Brazilians, and the Community of Portuguese Language Countries that was already being talked about was founded in 1996.

Madrid at 45: warm, and not warmer. The two joined the European Community together on 1 January 1986 and the frontier disappeared with it. Against that sit four hundred years in which Portuguese independence was defined as not being Spanish, an unrenounced Portuguese claim to Olivenza that both governments handle by never raising it, and a proverb about Spanish winds that every Portuguese schoolchild learns.

Ankara at -35 is the only substantially negative dyad in Western Europe and it is between two members of the same alliance. Turkey invaded Cyprus in July 1974 and 37% of the island was still occupied; the two states dispute the Aegean continental shelf, the width of Greek territorial waters, the extent of the Athens flight information region and the militarisation of the eastern islands; and on 27-28 March 1987 both navies put to sea over a survey ship and were talked down overnight. NATO has never contained a quarrel like it and this number should not pretend otherwise.

Washington at 25 is far below every other NATO member in this file, and deliberately. Andreas Papandreou won in 1981 on a platform of leaving NATO and closing the bases; he did neither, but the 1983 agreement was explicitly a withdrawal timetable, the Hellenikon and Nea Makri stations closed in 1991, and the American association with the junta of 1967-74 was a live domestic issue rather than history. The 17 November group had assassinated the CIA station chief Richard Welch in Athens in December 1975 and was still killing in 1990.

Moscow at 15 is higher than any other NATO member shows the Soviet Union, and that too is PASOK: Greece dissented from a long series of alliance positions in the 1980s and kept an open line to the Eastern bloc that Washington complained about repeatedly.

Israel at 5 is nearly nothing, and the date is the reason. Greece was the last member of the European Community to extend full de jure recognition to Israel, and did so only in May 1990 - four months into the game. Athens had backed the Palestinian position throughout the 1980s, partly on Arab oil and partly against Turkey.

Denmark is a founder member of NATO that spent the 1980s making the alliance uncomfortable. Between 1982 and 1988 a parliamentary majority of Social Democrats and the left forced the Schluter government to enter written reservations in twenty-three NATO communiques - the fodnotepolitik, the footnote policy - and in April 1988 the Folketing required visiting warships to confirm they carried no nuclear weapons, which is a demand no American or British ship is permitted to answer. The government called an election over it and won; the resolution was softened; and Washington sits at 45 here rather than at the 60 the Netherlands and Belgium show.
Norway at 70 is the union of 1380-1814 and the Nordic Council. Finland at 60 is slightly lower only because the Danish-Finnish relationship has no equivalent history behind it.

Norway is the most Atlanticist state in the Nordic region and the only one in this file that shows the Soviet Union a negative number. It holds NATO's northern flank: 196 kilometres of land border at Kirkenes and the sea approaches to the Northern Fleet's bases on Kola. United States Marine Corps equipment for a brigade had been prepositioned in Trondelag since 1981, and the Treholt affair of 1984, in which a senior foreign ministry official was convicted of spying for the KGB, was still fresh. Against that, Norway imposed self-limitations Moscow valued - no foreign bases and no nuclear weapons on Norwegian soil in peacetime - which is why the number is -10 and not -40.
London at 60 is the North Sea, the wartime alliance, and the fact that the Norwegian government spent 1940-45 in it.
Helsinki at 65, just below the Swedish and Danish 70s: a shared 736-kilometre border, a shared Arctic, and no history of governing one another.

Finland shows Moscow 45, the highest number any non-communist state in this entire file shows the Soviet Union, and it is the single most important entry in this block. The Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance of 6 April 1948 obliged Finland to resist an attack on the Soviet Union through Finnish territory, with Soviet assistance if needed, and it was still in force on 1 January 1990; it was terminated only in January 1992. A quarter of Finnish trade was with the Soviet Union under bilateral clearing arrangements, which is also why the Finnish depression of 1991-93 was as deep as it was - that trade simply stopped.

It is a warm number attached to a cold fact, and the model should read it as leverage rather than as friendship. Finland fought two wars against this neighbour between 1939 and 1944, lost 11% of its territory and evacuated 400,000 people from Karelia, and then spent forty-five years being extremely careful. Washington at 25 is the other side of that carefulness: correct, Western, and conspicuously not allied.
Stockholm, Oslo and Copenhagen were the direction Finland actually faced, and those numbers are in the Nordic blocks above.

London at 20 is the lowest number Ireland shows anybody and the only one that needs arguing. Read it against Spain-UK at 25 over Gibraltar, because the structure is the same and this quarrel is sharper: a constitutional claim on six counties in Articles 2 and 3, a war running in them that killed 76 people in 1990, an extradition regime the Irish courts kept refusing to operate, and the Birmingham Six still in English prisons - they were released on 14 March 1991. Against all that, the Anglo-Irish Agreement signed at Hillsborough on 15 November 1985 had given Dublin a formal consultative role in Northern Ireland for the first time since 1922, over the furious objection of every unionist party, and by 1990 the two governments were in constant contact. Positive, and thin, and the thinnest dyad in Western Europe outside Greece and Turkey.

Washington at 60 is the diaspora as an instrument of policy. Forty million Americans claimed Irish descent, the Friends of Ireland caucus was founded in 1981 by Tip O'Neill, Ted Kennedy and Daniel Patrick Moynihan, and the United States had underwritten the International Fund for Ireland since 1986. Ireland had an emigration problem in 1990 rather than an immigration one, and most of it went to New York and Boston.

Warsaw at 25 is higher than anything else Ireland shows the Eastern bloc, and it is Catholic solidarity: John Paul II had visited Ireland in 1979 and the Irish church raised money for Solidarity through the 1980s.

Czechoslovakia, six weeks after the Velvet Revolution and with Havel in the Castle. The warm lines run west and to the two neighbours it will found Visegrad with in February 1991; the line to Moscow is the coldest thing in this block that is not a war, because the first foreign-policy act of the new government was to demand that the Central Group of Forces leave, and the agreement to do it was signed on 26 February 1990 with the memory of August 1968 sitting on the table.

Washington at 55 is Havel's address to a joint session of Congress on 21 February 1990. Bonn at 40 rather than higher is deliberate: Havel opened 1990 by apologising for the expulsion of the Sudeten Germans, which improved nothing in Prague and settled nothing in Bavaria, and the property claims outlived both governments.
Beijing below zero is not an accident of the bloc breaking up. Havel received the Dalai Lama in Prague on 3 February 1990, the first head of state to do so, seven months after Tiananmen.

Hungary. Bonn at 55 is the highest number any nation in this region carries to a Western capital and it was earned in one night: on 10-11 September 1989 Hungary opened its Austrian border to the East Germans camped in Budapest, and the Wall came down nine weeks later. Kohl paid for it in credits and never stopped saying so.

Bucharest at minus 20 is the only negative line inside the former Warsaw Pact, and it is the reason Hungary's separatism figure can be 0.03: the strain is not inside Hungary's borders, it is across them. About 1.62 million Hungarians lived in Transylvania, UDMR was founded on 25 December 1989, and on 19-21 March 1990 Romanian and Hungarian crowds fought in Targu Mures with six dead - the first ethnic killing in post-communist Europe, eleven weeks into this start state.

Tel Aviv at 35 records a genuine first: Hungary restored full diplomatic relations with Israel on 18 September 1989, before any other Warsaw Pact member, twenty-two years after the bloc broke them together in 1967. Moscow at 15 is the same shape as Prague's and for the same reason - the withdrawal agreement for roughly 50,000 Soviet troops was signed on 10 March 1990.

Romania, and the two lines that look wrong until you check them. Israel at 45 is higher than any other former Warsaw Pact state carries, because Romania was the only member that never broke relations with Israel after the Six-Day War of 1967 - Ceausescu refused, kept the embassy open, and carried messages between Sadat and Begin before Camp David. The successor government inherited the channel intact. China at 40 is the same kind of fact from the other side: Bucharest took Beijing's part against Moscow from 1968 onward and was one of the few European capitals that did not condemn Tiananmen.

Washington at 15 is what is left after the United States withdrew most-favoured-nation status in 1988 over the systematisation of the villages, and after the Mineriad of June 1990 froze what the revolution had thawed. Moscow at 10 is a fair reading of a genuinely ambiguous dyad: Iliescu was Moscow-trained and the Front was widely suspected of Soviet sympathies, while the same Front's parliament was eighteen months away from declaring the Molotov-Ribbentrop pact void and demanding Bessarabia back.

Belgrade at 35 is the oldest warm line in this region: Romania was the one Warsaw Pact state that stayed close to Tito's Yugoslavia through the whole quarrel, and the two built the Iron Gates dams on the Danube together.

Bulgaria. Moscow at 45 is the warmest Soviet line in this matrix outside the successor states, and it is not sentiment: Bulgaria asked twice, in 1963 and 1973, to be admitted to the Soviet Union as a republic, ran about 60% of its trade through it, and was never invaded, purged or occupied because it never needed to be.

Ankara at minus 25 is the Revival Process. Between 1984 and 1989 the Bulgarian state forced Slavic names on roughly 800,000 Bulgarian Turks, and in the summer of 1989 it opened the frontier and drove some 340,000 of them across it - the largest forced movement of people in Europe since 1945, and the only such episode in this start state that had already happened rather than being about to. The policy was reversed on 29 December 1989, three days before the game opens, and reversing it brought Bulgarian nationalists into the streets of Sofia in January 1990.
Belgrade at 20 rather than 35 is Macedonia: Sofia would recognise the state early and the nation never.

Albania is the only nation in this roster with no ally of any kind on 1 January 1990, and these numbers are meant to look like that rather than like a small country with a modest foreign policy. It left the Warsaw Pact in 1968, denounced Moscow in 1961 and broke with Beijing in 1978, so it had spent twelve years quarrelling with every state large enough to protect it.

Belgrade at minus 20 is Kosovo, whose autonomy was stripped in March 1989 and whose demonstrators Yugoslav police shot in January and February 1990. It is the sharpest dyad in this region and the claim in nations.rs is its other half. MEASURED, and recorded here because the first figure entered was wrong and the model said so: this line was drafted at minus 35, which put Tirana and Belgrade level with Baghdad and Kuwait City in January 1990 - the one dyad in this file the appetite model is calibrated to turn into an invasion. It duly did, on seed 6: Yugoslavia invaded in April 1990 and annexed Albania in January 1991, a war that never happened and that nothing in the record suggests was close. Minus 20 is also the better transcription. The two states had ambassadors, a rail link opened in 1986, and Yugoslavia was among Albania's largest trading partners; the quarrel was loud, continuous, and conducted entirely through communiques.

Washington at minus 30 and London at minus 20 are not attitudes, they are the absence of relations: the United States had none with Albania from 1939 until 15 March 1991, and Britain none from 1946, when Albanian-laid mines in the Corfu Channel killed 44 Royal Navy sailors and the resulting ICJ judgement went unpaid for half a century. Moscow at minus 20 is the same fact with a date: relations broke in 1961 and were restored only on 30 July 1990, seven months after this start state. Beijing at 25 is what survives a break - the equipment, the doctrine and the habit outlasted the quarrel.

Latin America and Washington in 1990. The hemisphere has just finished changing shape: every South American state except Chile is under a civilian government for the first time since the 1950s, Chile's own transition is ten weeks from completion, and the debt crisis that defined the 1980s is being wound up one Brady agreement at a time. The United States is the unchallenged outside power and had just demonstrated it in Panama in December 1989, so the numbers here are warm rather than deferential - these are governments that want American money and American markets and are not being coerced into wanting them.

Menem's Argentina is the outlier at 55: he called it a carnal relationship, took Argentina out of the Non-Aligned Movement, wound up the Condor II missile programme, and sent the destroyer Almirante Brown and the corvette Spiro to the Gulf in September 1990 - the only Latin American state to join the coalition. Colombia at 45 is the drug war and the Cartagena summit of 15 February 1990. Mexico at 45 is Salinas asking for a free trade agreement in June 1990, against a century of keeping Washington at arm's length under the Estrada Doctrine. Venezuela at 45 is the largest oil supplier in the hemisphere and a Punto Fijo democracy in its thirty-second year.

Peru and Bolivia at 30 are the lowest of the nine and for the same reason: coca. Both were signatories at Cartagena and both were being paid to eradicate a crop their own peasantry lived on, which is a relationship with a permanent grievance inside it. Chile at 40 rather than higher is the Letelier assassination in Washington in 1976, still unprosecuted in January 1990 and still the reason for the Kennedy Amendment arms embargo.

Cuba, and the fact that the patron is dying. Thirty years of Soviet subsidy - sugar bought far above the world price, oil sold far below it, worth something like a quarter of Cuban national income - end when CMEA settlement moves to hard currency in January 1991. Moscow at 70 is the relationship as it stands in January 1990 and it is the most fragile number in this file; it should not survive the decade, and nothing here schedules its fall. Washington at -75 is the embargo, twenty-eight years old, with the Torricelli and Helms-Burton Acts still to come.

Mexico at 40 is the one that needs explaining: Mexico was the only member of the Organization of American States that refused to break relations with Havana after the 1964 sanctions, and kept the air link open for the whole period. Venezuela restored relations in 1974 and Carlos Andres Perez was personally close to Castro, which is worth 15 and no more, because Venezuela was also the hemisphere's loudest advocate of representative democracy as a condition of membership. Chile at -30 is Pinochet, who broke relations in September 1973 and had not restored them; Aylwin does so in 1990.

Beijing at 15 is a real relationship at a real distance. Havana had taken Moscow's side in the Sino-Soviet split and Castro had denounced China by name in 1966; the two had normal but cold relations by 1990, and it is the Soviet collapse rather than any warming that brings them together afterwards.

The quarrels inside the region, which are old, territorial, and mostly unresolved. Bolivia and Chile have had no ambassadors since 1978 over the Litoral, the coastline Bolivia lost in the War of the Pacific in 1879 and has demanded back every year since; the Bolivian navy still exists and still parades on the Dia del Mar. Peru and Ecuador dispute the Cordillera del Condor: Ecuador declared the 1942 Rio Protocol void in 1960, they shot at each other at Paquisha in 1981, and they fight the Cenepa war in January 1995 - which this dyad and the border in nations.rs are meant to make reachable without scripting it.

Colombia and Venezuela at -15 is the Gulf of Venezuela and the Los Monjes archipelago, a maritime delimitation that brought the corvette Caldas into disputed water in August 1987 and both air forces to readiness before anyone climbed down. Argentina and the United Kingdom at -20 is the Falklands: relations were restored on 19 February 1990 under the Madrid formula, with both sides agreeing to set sovereignty aside rather than settle it, so this is a cold dyad and not a hostile one.

Argentina and Chile at 35 is warm and recent, and it is the counter-example the region needs on the board: the 1984 Treaty of Peace and Friendship ended the Beagle Channel crisis that had come within hours of war in December 1978, and twenty-two of the twenty-four remaining boundary segments are settled by agreement in August 1991. Two states with an old border quarrel can also simply stop.

The two integration projects the region is building in 1990, which is what most of the warm intra-regional numbers are. Brazil and Argentina at 60 is the largest reversal in South American diplomatic history: two states that had spent the 1970s racing each other toward a bomb signed the Iguacu Declaration on nuclear policy in 1985, opened each other's enrichment plants to mutual inspection, signed the Buenos Aires Act on 6 July 1990 setting a common market for 1995, and brought in Uruguay and Paraguay at Asuncion in March 1991. The Foz do Iguacu declaration of 28 November 1990 renounced nuclear weapons outright.

The other project is the Andean Pact, relaunched by the Galapagos Declaration of December 1989 after a decade of paralysis: Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Venezuela, hence the block of thirties between them. Note what these numbers do NOT say - Ecuador and Peru are both in the pact and are at -45 with each other, because a trade bloc is not a friendship and the model should not be told otherwise.

Madrid and the Americas, which is the second axis of Spanish foreign policy in this period and the one the Spain block above names without pricing. The first Ibero-American Summit meets at Guadalajara on 18 July 1991 on a joint Spanish and Mexican initiative, and the run-up to the 1992 quincentenary is why Spanish investment banks and telephone companies arrive in the region in this decade rather than another one.

Spain and Cuba at 20 is the entry that carries information. Spain never joined the American embargo, was Cuba's largest Western trading partner and its largest source of tourists, and had a relationship built on roughly a million Cubans of recent Spanish descent - and it was also a European democracy with an ambassador who kept meeting dissidents, so the two governments spent the decade quarrelling and never breaking. A warm number would be as wrong as a cold one.

Argentina at 45 is above the rest for the sheer weight of the Spanish community in Buenos Aires and the fact that Madrid brokered the Falklands restoration of relations in February 1990 in its own capital, which is what the Madrid formula is named after.

The Middle East on 1 January 1990: eight nations added, and the arithmetic of a region seven months before the Gulf crisis rearranged all of it. Every dyad below is stated once, and the pairs already in this file are not restated - Iraq-Kuwait at -35, Iraq-Saudi at -25, Iraq-Iran at -50, USA-Saudi at 50, USA-Iraq at -20, USA-Iran at -60 and UK-Kuwait at 50 all stand as written above.

Syria is the outlier of Arab politics in this period and its numbers are meant to look strange. Damascus and Baghdad were the two wings of the same party and hated each other more than either hated anyone else: Syria was the only Arab state to back Iran through all eight years of the Iran-Iraq war, closed the Kirkuk-Banias pipeline against Baghdad in 1982, and joined the coalition against Iraq in 1990. Hence Syria-Iraq at -60, the most hostile pair in this block and worse than either state's line to Israel. Syria-Iran at 55 is that same alliance from the other end, between a secular Ba'athist republic and an Islamic one, and it has outlasted every prediction made about it. Syria-Israel at -70 is the Golan and the Bekaa Valley air battle of June 1982, in which Syria lost eighty-two aircraft and Israel none. Syria-Turkey at -30 is water and the PKK: the Ataturk Dam closed the Euphrates for a month in January 1990 to fill its reservoir, and Damascus was hosting Abdullah Ocalan while it complained about it.

Lebanon's numbers are the numbers of a country other people were fighting in. Lebanon-Syria at 35 is not friendship; it is the reading of a state whose president had been installed under the Taif Accord of October 1989 with Syrian backing, and whose rival government was destroyed by the Syrian assault of 13 October 1990. Lebanon-Israel at -50 is the security zone north of the 1978 line. Lebanon-France at 30 is the mandate, the language and the paratroopers of the 1982-84 multinational force.

Jordan is the pivot that broke. King Hussein was the closest Arab ally London and Washington had after Cairo, and then declined to join the coalition against Iraq, because Jordan bought its oil from Baghdad down the desert highway and several hundred thousand of its people worked in the Gulf. The Jordan-Iraq line therefore opens POSITIVE at 40, which is the fact that made 1990-91 so expensive for Amman, and Jordan-Saudi opens at 30 with further to fall than any other pair here.

The Gulf monarchies are a bloc that does not quite hold together yet. The Co-operation Council was eight years old in 1990; its members are entered warm to one another and warmer to Washington and London, whose treaties with the Trucial States ran to 1971 and whose habits outlasted them - Oman-UK at 70 is the highest number in this block, and it is the Sultan's Armed Forces' British officers, the Dhofar War and the facilities at Masirah. Two exceptions are deliberate. Qatar-Bahrain at 10 is barely positive because of the Hawar Islands and the Fasht al-Dibal raid of 26 April 1986, the only near-war between Council members. And Yemen sits outside the bloc entirely: Yemen-Saudi at -25 is the Treaty of Taif claim on Asir, Jizan and Najran, a frontier nobody had demarcated, and a million Yemeni workers held on sufferance; Yemen-USSR at 55 is the inheritance of Aden, Moscow's only Arabian client and its facility at Socotra.

Iran and the Arab shore. Iran-UAE at -20 is Abu Musa and the Tunbs, taken on 30 November 1971. Iran-Bahrain at -30 is the coup attempt of December 1981 by the Islamic Front for the Liberation of Bahrain, which Bahrain's courts found had been trained in Iran, and behind it the Shah's claim to the whole island - dropped in 1970 and not forgotten by anybody living on it. Iran-Oman at 25 is the odd one and it is real: Iranian troops fought for the Sultan in Dhofar from 1973, Muscat stayed neutral through the Iran-Iraq war, and the two states share the Strait of Hormuz and have always talked.

North Africa, and the first thing the numbers have to carry is that the Maghreb in January 1990 was in the middle of a reconciliation, not a quarrel. The Arab Maghreb Union treaty was signed at Marrakesh on 17 February 1989 by all five of these states; Algeria and Morocco had restored diplomatic relations in May 1988 after twelve years and reopened the frontier; Tunisia and Libya had restored theirs in December 1987. A table that opened these dyads cold would be modelling 1984, not 1990.

What is not warm is Algiers-Rabat, and the reason is a country that is not in this roster. Algeria armed and housed the Polisario Front at Tindouf; Morocco held the Western Sahara behind a 2,700km sand wall. The two were AMU partners and proxy belligerents at the same time, which is what a modestly positive number between two neighbours who will not fight each other directly is meant to express.

Libya is the outlier in every direction. Moscow was its arms supplier and Washington had bombed it in April 1986; London had broken relations over the killing of Yvonne Fletcher in 1984 and Paris had fought it by proxy in Chad until 1987. Rome is the exception among the Western powers and the exception is commercial: ENI's gas and Italy's position as Libya's largest trading partner outweighed a colonial history worse than anything France left in the Maghreb.

Khartoum's alignment had just moved. The coup of 30 June 1989 cost it the American aid relationship and much of Saudi Arabia's patience, and it turned instead to the two capitals that would take it: Tripoli, which supplied oil and arms and had helped bring the regime in, and after that Baghdad and Tehran. That is the shape of the Sudanese row below, and it is also why Sudan will not behave like Egypt when the Gulf crisis arrives.

Cairo-Tripoli deserves its own line. These two fought a four-day war in July 1977 and Libya spent the Sadat years sponsoring attempts on his life; Mubarak and Gaddafi were nonetheless publicly reconciled in October 1989, border restrictions lifted and hundreds of thousands of Egyptians working in Libya. A small positive number is the honest reading of a relationship that is functional and one incident from not being.

SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA, block 1 of 11 (branch feat/r-ssafrica): South Africa. Every dyad in this regional set is stated exactly once, and the blocks are ordered so that a nation only names partners that have not already had a block of their own.

Apartheid South Africa in January 1990 is the most isolated state in this roster and the arithmetic should show it. It had left the Commonwealth in 1961 rather than be expelled, was under a mandatory UN arms embargo since Resolution 418 of 4 November 1977, and had been under American sanctions since the Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act passed over Reagan's veto on 2 October 1986. India had severed relations in 1946, the first country in the world to do so, and led the campaign at the UN for forty years; Nigeria funded the ANC and chaired the anti-apartheid caucus; Tanzania hosted the ANC's camps and Nyerere built the Frontline States around opposing Pretoria.

The positive numbers are the interesting ones and they are all real. London stays warmest of the Western capitals because Thatcher opposed comprehensive sanctions to the end and British investment never left. Israel is the outlier at 55: an arms relationship that survived the 1977 embargo and outlasted everyone else's, and the only country whose cooperation with Pretoria deepened in the 1980s. Zaire is positive because Mobutu and Pretoria were on the same side in Angola for fifteen years, supplying UNITA through Kamina.

Angola at -60 is the lowest line South Africa has, and it is the only one that was a shooting war: the SADF fought FAPLA and the Cubans at Cuito Cuanavale through 1987-88. The Tripartite Accord of 22 December 1988 ended it and Namibia became independent on 21 March 1990, eleven weeks into the game, so this number is the one most likely to be moving already.

Block 2 of 11: Ethiopia. A Soviet client, and one of the two most heavily armed ones in the third world — Moscow supplied the Derg from 1977, switching sides from Somalia mid-war in the Ogaden, and had delivered something over $10bn of equipment by 1990. That is the single most important line in this block and it is also the one about to fail: Gorbachev told Mengistu the arms agreement would not be renewed past 1990, and the government fell in May 1991.

Kenya at 45 is the oldest alignment in East Africa and it is a negative one — the mutual defence understanding of 1964 existed because both states had a Somali irredentist claim against them. Israel at 40 is likewise concrete rather than sentimental: military assistance in exchange for the emigration of Ethiopian Jews, which produced Operation Solomon and 14,325 people flown out of Addis Ababa in 36 hours on 24-25 May 1991, as the EPRDF entered the city.
Egypt is negative and the Nile is the whole of it. Ethiopia's highlands supply about 85% of the Blue Nile's water and Egypt had spent the century insisting on the colonial-era allocations.

Block 3 of 11: Kenya. The most Western-aligned state in East Africa and deliberately so — Britain kept training rights, and the United States had had access to Mombasa for the Indian Ocean since the 1980 facilities agreement, which was what made Kenya strategically worth the aid. That access is why Washington's line here is high and why the aid suspension of November 1991 over governance was such a departure.

Tanzania at only 15 is a real coolness and not an oversight. The East African Community collapsed in 1977 in mutual recrimination over the distribution of its assets, and Nyerere closed the Kenyan border for six years — capitalist Kenya and Ujamaa Tanzania were the two models being compared, and each side knew it. Uganda at 20 carries the border clashes of December 1987, when the two armies exchanged fire at Busia.

Block 4 of 11: Ghana. Nkrumah's non-alignment is a generation gone; the PNDC of 1990 is the IMF's favourite African client and its foreign policy follows the money. Nigeria at 20 rather than higher is the one line that needs stating: Lagos expelled up to two million West Africans in January 1983 and again in April 1985, the great majority of them Ghanaians, and it is not a thing a country forgets in five years. They were nonetheless both in ECOWAS and both sent troops to ECOMOG in Liberia that August.

Block 5 of 11: Zaire. The most valuable Western client in Africa and the least defensible one: Mobutu was flown to power with Belgian and American help, kept there through two Shaba invasions by French and Moroccan troops on American aircraft, and used as the conduit for arms to UNITA through the Kamina base. Washington and Paris both sit at the top of this block for that reason and both cut him loose within eighteen months of the game's start — Belgium suspended aid after the Lubumbashi killings of 11-12 May 1990, and the United States ended military assistance in November 1990.

Angola at -40 is the mirror of block 6: Kinshasa backed the FNLA and then UNITA for fifteen years, and Luanda backed the Katangese gendarmes who invaded Shaba in 1977 and 1978. Neither ever claimed the other's ground, which is why nations.rs records no claim between them and why the number is a hostility rather than a war.

Block 6 of 11: Angola. The deepest Soviet commitment in Africa outside Ethiopia, and the only one with 50,000 Cuban troops attached to it — they arrived in November 1975 and the last left on 25 May 1991 under the New York Accords. Moscow at 80 is the highest single line this regional block contains.

Washington at -40 is the Reagan Doctrine as it actually ran: the Clark Amendment was repealed in July 1985 and covert aid to Savimbi resumed, delivered through Zaire, while the United States withheld diplomatic recognition from Luanda until 1993 — which is remarkable given that Chevron was pumping Cabinda's oil the whole time and paying the MPLA government for it. China is negative for the reason nobody expects: Beijing armed the FNLA and then UNITA against a Soviet-backed MPLA, which is the Sino-Soviet split fought out in Angola.

The African lines are warm across the board. Angola was a Frontline State, the OAU recognised the MPLA government from 1976, and Zimbabwe and Tanzania both read Savimbi as Pretoria's instrument, which for most of the 1980s he was.

Block 7 of 11: Zimbabwe. The most interesting line here is Moscow's, and it is low. The Soviet Union backed ZAPU and Joshua Nkomo through the liberation war; China armed and trained ZANLA, Mugabe's wing, from 1971. ZANU won, and Zimbabwe's relations with the two communist powers in 1990 are the inverse of what a map of the Cold War would predict — Beijing at 55, Moscow at 10. This is exactly the sort of fact a per-pair table invents wrong and a transcribed one gets right.

Britain at 45 is Lancaster House and the settlement that produced independence on 18 April 1980, plus the land-purchase money that came with it and had not yet become the quarrel it became. Tanzania at 55 is the Frontline States, whose meetings Nyerere chaired and where Zimbabwe was the newest and most important member.

Block 8 of 11: Tanzania. China at 70 is the highest non-Soviet line in this regional set and it is earned in concrete: the TAZARA railway, 1,860km from Dar es Salaam to the Zambian copperbelt, built between 1970 and 1975 by some 25,000 Chinese workers and financed by an interest-free loan — the largest single foreign aid project China had undertaken anywhere, and built precisely so that Zambia's copper would not have to leave through Rhodesia or South Africa. Non-alignment with a very clear direction of travel.
Uganda at 20 rather than higher: Tanzania invaded in 1979, took Kampala and restored Obote, whom the NRM then spent five years fighting. Gratitude and grievance in the same dyad.

Block 9 of 11: Uganda. Four years into the NRM and rebuilding its foreign relations from a very low base — Britain and the United States are the donors underwriting the recovery programme and their lines reflect that rather than any strategic weight. The relationship the sim cannot see because Rwanda is not in this roster is the one that mattered most: the Rwandan Patriotic Front invaded Rwanda on 1 October 1990 out of Uganda, its senior officers serving in the NRA when they left.

Block 10 of 11: Senegal. France at 80 is the closest bilateral relationship any African state in this roster has with a European one, and it is institutional rather than sentimental: a defence agreement dating from 1974, a French garrison at Ouakam outside Dakar, and a currency issued by a central bank whose parity the French Treasury guaranteed. If the sim's patronage machinery is going to produce a French sphere in Africa, this is the dyad it should be built on.

Iraq at -25 is not a historical curiosity: Senegal sent about 500 troops to the coalition in the Gulf, and 92 of them were killed when their aircraft crashed near Ras al-Mishab returning home on 21 March 1991 — the largest single loss Senegal has ever suffered. Saudi Arabia at 45 is the other half of that alignment and the Islamic-solidarity funding behind it.

Block 11 of 11: Cameroon. The other franc-zone member here, with the same French architecture as Senegal — defence accords, a guaranteed currency, and a president who visited Paris more often than his own northern provinces. Slightly below Senegal's 80 because Cameroon's independence quarrel was bloodier: France fought the UPC insurgency into the mid-1960s and the party's founder Ruben Um Nyobe was killed by French troops in 1958, which is why the UPC sits in the government.rs party table as a legalised opposition rather than as a partner.

Nigeria at 15 is low and it is the Bakassi claim in nations.rs seen from the diplomatic side: a live territorial dispute with a neighbour ten times your size, with naval incidents in May 1981 that nearly became a war. Cameroon filed at the International Court of Justice on 29 March 1994 rather than fight, which is the correct reading of a 0.003 claim against a strength ratio of four to one.

South Asia, and the organising fact is that every one of these states defines itself against India rather than against a bloc. The Cold War alignment that structures the European and Middle Eastern blocks above barely reaches here; what does the structuring is that India is larger than all its neighbours combined, and each of them keeps China somewhere in reserve because of it. That is why Beijing scores 40-55 with Dhaka, Colombo, Kathmandu and Rangoon alike while Washington and Moscow score middling numbers with all four.

Bangladesh is warmer with China and Japan than with the country that created it. The 1971 debt was real and is spent by 1990: Ershad had tilted deliberately toward Beijing, Islamabad and the Islamic world, and the open files with Delhi were the Farakka barrage and the dry-season flow of the Ganges, the Tin Bigha corridor, and the Chakma refugees the Hill Tracts war pushed into Tripura. Japan is high because it was the largest bilateral aid donor.

Sri Lanka's negative with India is the sharpest number in this block and it is recent. The Indian Peace Keeping Force arrived in 1987 under an accord Colombo signed under duress, ended up fighting the Tamil Tigers it had come to disarm, and Premadasa campaigned on expelling it - the last troops left on 24 March 1990. Two states that were not at war and whose relationship was nonetheless worse than either had with anyone else in the region.

Nepal at -20 with India is the other blockade in this table. The trade and transit treaties lapsed on 23 March 1989 and Delhi closed twenty-one of twenty-three border crossings; a landlocked country lost its fuel, and the proximate cause was Kathmandu buying anti-aircraft guns from China in 1988. The Chinese number and the Indian number here are the same event seen from two ends.

Afghanistan is the one entry in this block that is a Cold War position rather than a South Asian one, and it carries the most extreme values in this file after Iraq's. Najibullah's government existed because Moscow paid for it, and everyone arming the men trying to kill it is scored accordingly: Pakistan ran the pipeline through the ISI, Saudi Arabia matched American funding dollar for dollar, and Washington's Operation Cyclone was the largest covert programme in its history. India is the outlier at +45 and it is not an error - Delhi recognised and supported the Kabul government throughout, alone in South Asia, for the straightforward reason that Islamabad was the alternative.

Myanmar had just changed patrons. SLORC crushed the 1988 uprising, was embargoed by the West, and China stepped in - the border trade agreement of 1988 and a very large arms relationship followed, which is the +55 here and the beginning of the dependency that defined Burma for the next twenty years. Japan sits positive despite suspending aid, because it had been the largest donor for decades and was the first to resume.

The two Koreas and the two Chinas: four states whose foreign policy in January 1990 is mostly about denying recognition to a fifth. Pyongyang's patrons are Beijing and Moscow, and Moscow is about to defect - Shevardnadze went to Pyongyang in September 1990 to say the Soviet Union would recognise Seoul, and Kim Yong Nam told him to his face that it would push the North toward building its own bomb. Taipei's position is the mirror image and it is why the number with Washington is warm rather than allied: the United States switched recognition to Beijing on 1 January 1979 and went on selling Taiwan weapons anyway under the Taiwan Relations Act, which is a relationship with no embassy in it.

Cross-strait is entered at -50 and the anchors either side of it are in this same file. It is below the United States and the Soviet Union at -45, because Beijing has never renounced the use of force and Taipei was still governing under a statute for the suppression of a rebellion. It is above India and Pakistan at -55 and Iraq and Iran at -50, because nothing had been fired across the strait since the Kinmen shelling stopped on 1 January 1979, family visits had been legal since 1987, indirect trade through Hong Kong ran to billions a year, and the machinery for talks was built during 1990 itself - the National Unification Council in October and the Straits Exchange Foundation in November. An armed standoff in its thaw year, not a war in its interval.

This region ships only the dyads it would be a misrepresentation to omit. The trade and aid warmth that also existed - Japanese investment across ASEAN, the Commonwealth ties to Kuala Lumpur and Singapore, the Five Power Defence Arrangements - is left out on purpose. Those have no figure behind them the way a severed recognition or a signed treaty does, and a dense mesh of invented mid-range friendship is not free: patronage and intervention both read this matrix, so inventing warmth redirects the great powers' budgets and the coalitions they join.

Indochina and the states around it. Vietnam's two junior partners are still junior: the Lao People's Revolutionary Party came out of the same movement as the Vietnamese party and signed a twenty-five-year treaty of friendship with Hanoi in 1977, and the State of Cambodia was installed by the Vietnamese army in 1979 and had watched it march home four months before the game opens. Thailand is the other side of that war - it sheltered the resistance coalition, the Khmer Rouge included, along the Aranyaprathet border, and Chatichai's line about turning Indochina from a battlefield into a marketplace was in 1988 the first crack in that policy rather than the end of it.

Laos sits badly with both of its large neighbours for dated reasons. Vientiane took Hanoi's side when China and Vietnam went to war in 1979 and Chinese aid stopped; relations were only restored in 1989. And Thailand and Laos had fought each other over three villages on the Sainyabuli border from December 1987 to February 1988, which is the claim entered in the roster and the reason this pair is not neutral.

Mongolia's foreign relations in January 1990 consist almost entirely of the Soviet Union, whose 39th Army is still on its territory and whose transfers ran near a third of its output. The figure with China is low and positive rather than hostile: the rupture of the 1960s was formally closed by the normalisation of 1989, and the border treaty of 1962 was never in dispute.

Bangkok and Manila hold American defence treaties dating to 1954 and 1951. Kuala Lumpur and Manila are on speaking terms and do not discuss Sabah, which is why that pair is mildly warm and not hostile despite the claim in the roster - the claim is live, the quarrel is shelved, and those are different facts.

Canada in January 1990 is the most closely tied nation on this board to the most powerful one, and the 85 with Washington is the highest single number in this file. NORAD had put continental air defence under a joint command since 1958, the Canada-United States Free Trade Agreement had been in force since 1 January 1989, and the two are NATO allies with a Canadian mechanised brigade and air division standing in Germany. Nothing else Canada has comes close, and much of Canadian foreign policy in this period is an attempt to have something else.

Paris is the exception among the Western capitals and Quebec is the whole of the reason. De Gaulle's 'Vive le Quebec libre' from the balcony of Montreal city hall in 1967 was a French head of state endorsing the breakup of a NATO ally on its own soil, and France has maintained a direct relationship with Quebec City ever since. Entered at 40, below Germany and Japan - which looks like an odd ranking until you remember that the Canadian brigade was at Lahr and Baden-Soellingen and that Japan was the second-largest customer.

Delhi is the coldest line Canada has with a democracy and it is 15 rather than 60 for two specific reasons. India's 1974 test used plutonium from the CIRUS reactor Canada had supplied for civil research, and Canada cut off nuclear cooperation over it. And Air India 182 was blown out of the sky off Ireland in June 1985 by a bomb loaded in Vancouver - the largest mass murder in Canadian history, and still being prosecuted twenty years later.

The Commonwealth pair are stated here so that they are stated once: Australia 70 and New Zealand 65 are shared institutions, a shared head of state, and no shared interest urgent enough to make either number higher.

Australia's alliance is real and unqualified: ANZUS in force, and the joint facilities at Pine Gap and Nurrungar doing work for the United States that no other ally's territory did. 78 rather than Canada's 85 only because there is no NORAD and no free trade agreement, not because there is any doubt.

Japan at 62 records something people forget about 1990: Japan had been Australia's largest export market since 1966, and the iron ore of the Pilbara and the coking coal of the Bowen Basin went almost entirely there. The economic relationship overtook the imperial one two decades before the sentimental one caught up, which is why this number sits within six points of Britain's.

China at 35 is a relationship in its worst state since recognition in 1972. Hawke wept on national television reading the casualty reports from Beijing on 9 June 1989 and extended the visas of some 42,000 Chinese students already in Australia, which Beijing treated as Beijing treats such things.

Indonesia at 42 is cooperative and squalid in equal measure. Australia was the only Western state to recognise the annexation of East Timor de jure, and Gareth Evans and Ali Alatas signed the Timor Gap Treaty dividing the seabed on 11 December 1989 - in a light aircraft circling over the Timor Sea, because there was no agreed coastline to sign it on. A working relationship between two states that do not like each other, which is what a number in the forties is for.

France at 12 is the atmospheric testing at Mururoa, which Australia and New Zealand jointly took to the International Court of Justice in 1973. Entered well above New Zealand's negative figure because Australia's grievance is a policy and New Zealand's is a killing, and because the Matignon Accords of 1988 had defused New Caledonia, which was the other half of it.

This block exists for one number. New Zealand and the United States open at 20 - below New Zealand and China, and only five above New Zealand and the Soviet Union - and that is neither a mistake nor a modelling choice. The Fourth Labour Government banned nuclear-armed and nuclear-powered warship visits, refused the USS Buchanan in February 1985, and Washington formally suspended its ANZUS security obligations to New Zealand in August 1986: downgraded from ally to friend, intelligence sharing cut, ministerial contact suspended. The ban was entrenched in the New Zealand Nuclear Free Zone, Disarmament, and Arms Control Act 1987, and by 1990 both major parties had accepted it. Two democracies of nearly identical outlook, and the alliance between them is switched off. A roster that means to cover the world has to be able to hold that, and a hand-enumerated table of blocs cannot.

France at -30 is the only negative number any of these three nations carries, and it is the Rainbow Warrior. Two DGSE agents bombed a Greenpeace vessel at its berth in Auckland Harbour on 10 July 1985 and killed the photographer Fernando Pereira - a state attack on a civilian target in the port of a friendly country. They were convicted of manslaughter, transferred to the French base at Hao under a UN-brokered settlement, and returned to France early in breach of it, the last of them in May 1988. Eighteen months before the game starts.

Britain at 62 is warm and diminished, and 1973 is why: the United Kingdom joined the European Economic Community and New Zealand lost the guaranteed access for butter and lamb that had been most of its economy since refrigerated shipping began in 1882. The relationship survived it. The trade did not.

Australia at 85 is stated in the Australian block above and not repeated here. It is the only alliance New Zealand has left, and Closer Economic Relations since 1983 makes it an economic union in all but name.

Small and island Europe. Four states with a combined output smaller than Denmark's and a combined population smaller than Dublin's, and the reason each of them gets a block rather than being left to the region default is that three of the four are aligned in a way their geography does not predict.

Iceland is the extreme case in this roster of alignment without armament. It has never had armed forces, and it was a FOUNDER member of NATO in 1949 - the only one without an army - because Keflavik sits on the GIUK gap and the United States kept roughly 3,000 personnel there under the defence agreement of 5 May 1951. Iceland and the USA at 78 is therefore higher than the number for several states with real armies, and it is the correct reading: the whole of Icelandic security policy is that relationship. The UK at 45 is the one number here that is held DOWN rather than up, and the reason is the Cod Wars: three confrontations between Icelandic coast guard cutters and Royal Navy frigates over the fisheries limit, in 1958, 1972-73 and 1975-76, the last of which ended with Reykjavik breaking diplomatic relations with London on 19 February 1976 and threatening to leave NATO. Two allies of thirty years and the lower number is the ally. The USSR at 25 is warmer than a NATO member's default because Iceland sold the Soviet Union fish through the whole Cold War and Reykjavik hosted the Reagan-Gorbachev summit in October 1986.

Luxembourg is the least surprising row in this file and it is entered because its absence would be read as distance. Founder member of the United Nations, NATO, the European Coal and Steel Community, the EEC and Benelux; in monetary union with Belgium at fixed parity since 1921, which is why Belgium at 88 is the highest bilateral number Luxembourg carries and one of the highest in this file.

Malta is the interesting one, and every number in its row is lower than a Western European reflex would put it. Malta in January 1990 is a member of the Non-Aligned Movement with neutrality written into Article 1 of its constitution by the amendment of 1987. The Royal Navy left Grand Harbour on 31 March 1979 after 179 years, and Dom Mintoff spent the years after that signing a treaty of friendship with Libya, taking neutrality guarantees from Italy and from the Soviet Union, and putting Maltese foreign policy as far from London as it would go. Eddie Fenech Adami turned it back toward Europe from 1987 and applied to join the European Community on 16 July 1990, but he did it without leaving non-alignment. Hence Italy at 70 - the 1980 guarantee, and the nearest neighbour - against the UK at 45, Libya at 40 and the USSR at 25. The Bush-Gorbachev summit was held aboard ship off Marsaxlokk on 2-3 December 1989, five weeks before this start state, and Malta being an acceptable venue to both superpowers is the whole point of the row.

Cyprus is the row where the numbers are a war. Turkey invaded on 20 July 1974 and 30,000-35,000 Turkish troops were still on the island in January 1990, so -80 is the second most hostile pair in this file and the roster row carries the matching claim. Greece at 85 is enosis without the annexation - the Greek Cypriot state's guarantor, patron and identity - and it is high enough to make the Greece-Turkey-Cyprus triangle behave as the single object it was. The UK at 30 is the one that needs explaining: Britain is a guarantor power under the Treaty of Guarantee of 1960, it holds 254 square kilometres of sovereign base area at Akrotiri and Dhekelia, and it did not intervene in 1974. A guarantor that did not guarantee scores like a neutral. The USSR at 45 is higher than any other Western-facing state in this batch gives Moscow, and it is not sentiment: the Soviet Union backed the Republic's territorial position at the United Nations consistently from 1974, and AKEL - a communist party polling 27% - ran the largest trade union federation on the island and elected the sitting president in 1988. The USA at 5 is the cost of Washington's role in 1974, which Greek Cypriots have never forgiven and which is why the number is barely off zero rather than warm.
